notes.1: Question 1: A senior officer asks Muller to give an account of his meeting with the criminal the previous day. He asks Muller the following three questions only: Why did you take the reckless decision to go alone to meet Sorensen? What was your physical and mental state before the meeting? What happened in the next few minutes after the door opened? Write the words of the interview. [20 marks] Most candidates wrote recognisable interviews and showed that they understood the need to adopt the detective’s viewpoint and attitudes. Higher scoring responses were able to explore the idea that Muller wanted to make up for the past and do his job professionally and effectively. Muller’s reasons for going alone were all to do with his knowledge of the criminal and the necessity of following his instructions, though these could be contained within the presentation of his character as a rule-bending maverick. Some responses had unnecessarily long introductions, and some gave the answers to the three questions as an uninterrupted monologue. The interview was conducted by a ‘senior officer’, and a chatty dialogue between equals was not the most appropriate register for an official interrogation. Details of the previous occasion when Sorensen was involved with the police provided necessary background material, and could be skilfully woven into an explanation of Muller’s curiosity and decision to meet the criminal on this occasion. It is worth noting that information given in the introduction to passages should be read, and utilised where relevant. Some responses had not understood that Sorensen had broken into a summer house, and therefore as it was not his house, no conclusions about him could be drawn from the appearance or state of it. It also made it hard to explain Muller’s difficulty in finding his way there. Other responses wrongly assumed it was the setting of the armed robbery with hostages ten years previously, and went on to claim that the property had a secret passage or exit. Several responses showed a misreading of the significance of 4 pm, the deadline by which Muller had to be there because Sorensen intended to leave, not arrive, at that time. Less confident responses made little attempt to adapt the material. In such cases the first and second sections contained plain facts about the distant and/or recent past. They needed to include information about the context and move beyond the ideas of fear and danger. Muller’s complex and changing feelings in the lead up to the opening of the door were not always appreciated, and this section in particular would have benefitted from using own words rather than lifting key phrases from the passage, or the presenting of events in an order other than chronological. Some first sections required structure and cohesion of details to convey a clear picture of Muller’s decision to go alone. On occasions, Muller gave his reason as the need to rescue hostages, often his own children; this idea was not convincingly tethered to the known facts and distorted the real focus, sometimes giving Muller an inappropriately maniacal and vengeful voice. Some second sections would have benefitted from reconciling Muller’s nervousness with his determination. The ‘spinning of wheels’ was sometimes misinterpreted as Muller’s bad driving rather than being attributed to the mud and weather conditions. Some responses needed to able to select and make use of the fact that Muller deliberately exposed himself to Sorensen’s view from the window of the house, knowing he could be seen. Weaker responses did not address the third bullet at all, typically preventing the award of a mark higher than the middle of Band 3. The obvious inference to be made was that Sorensen would once again perform a disappearing act as part of his continuing desire to prove himself cleverer than the police. In good responses, references to what had already happened and had been said were the basis of expectations for the future. While the suicide, surrender or arrest of Sorensen were plausible outcomes, an abject apology and desire to tell all and be forgiven was rather less so. Most of the marks for this question were given for showing understanding of the passage and for using ideas within the framework of the response, which was provided in the sequence of questions. It was not possible to use all the details from the passage in the space available, but good responses included all the main ones, to do with the landscape and weather conditions, the known history of the criminal, and the ill omens around the house. Effective planning ensured that there was no repetition between sections and that they were all given equal attention and coverage. The use of ideas demonstrates explicit understanding, whereas the use of detail is necessary to show close reading, and development proves implicit understanding. Responses need to convey all three levels of reading comprehension to attain the higher band marks. In less good answers there were examples of copying whole phrases and sentences from the passage, and sometimes several lines were lifted with virtually no changes in the wording. The more the content of the passage was adapted to the genre and focus of the question, the more likely it was that the mark for reading would be high. Reponses were most prone to lifting in section two, without exploration and expansion upon Muller’s complex state of mind. Better responses referred to his tension, his apprehension, his vulnerability, his distrust, his desire to ensure that Sorensen remained in control, and his realisation that no help was available in such a bleak and remote place. Where the third section was attempted, weaker responses re-iterated material from the previous section, about his fear of what Sorensen might do, or introduced other characters in the form of henchmen and hostages, for which there was no expectation in the passage, or constructed a series of events involving guns and killings, or the hospitalisation of Muller. A more subtle drama was added to the third section by the use of convincing direct speech uttered by Sorensen, particularly when related to known previous facts, such as that he had been ordered to come alone. Better responses developed the implicit ideas that the Skoda, the trees or the weather would play a role in the outcome, or that Sorensen would, on past showing, be likely to be armed. Most of the responses which addressed the third question followed the instruction to limit the events to the next few minutes, although some allowed Muller and Sorensen to have a tour of the house, or a drink and a meal together, which went beyond this time frame. The writing mark reflected the clarity and fluency of the interview, and how well it used vivid language to capture the sense of the drama of the experience and the character of the protagonist. Rhetorical questions were neither plausible in the linguistic context nor an effective means of conveying information. The better written responses had a lively, engaging and convincing style, and the personality and views of the interviewer did not overwhelm the informative content or detract from the central focus. Here are some ways in which this type of response could be improved: ● Answer all parts of the question. ● Answer in your own words and adapt material from the passage to the type of response you are writing. ● Be aware of the main issues and themes in the passage and use plenty of detail to support your ideas. ● Create a suitable voice and tone to show your understanding of what you have read.
notes.2: Question 2: Re-read the descriptions of (a) the landscape in paragraph 2, and (b) the house and surroundings in paragraph 4. Select words and phrases from these descriptions, and explain how the writer has created effects by using this language. [10 marks] It was necessary for marks in the top two bands to focus on the chosen language at word level. Most responses included some relevant choices, including imagery, in both paragraphs. Section (b) was less well answered because the choices and effects were a little less obvious. The bright paint and homely furniture could be interpreted as an ironic contrast to the general surroundings and situation, as being sinisterly misleading, or as a mixture of the pleasant and unpleasant, summer and winter, good and evil. It was important not to give a general description of the landscape and venue. There was some evidence that candidates stopped when they thought they had written enough, without considering the balance of their response. Nearly all responses said something about the ‘dead country towns’ in paragraph 2 (sometimes trying to equate them with the wild west or horror movies, or to claim them as a foreshadowing of death) and the ‘red- yellow ochre’ colour in paragraph 4. Few selected the ‘black stripes of earth’ or ‘blades rotating synchronously’ in paragraph 2, though these lent themselves to exploration of other avenues of the colourless or intimidating landscape and atmosphere. In paragraph 4, ‘near-withered hollyhocks’ was not chosen as a possible choice in most responses, though it is clear that plants are being referred to and their withering could have been linked to the end of Sorensen’s criminal career, the threat of death possibly A frequent choice was ‘clumps hanging over Muller, or simply to the season of autumn and what it evokes. of weather-worn’ which was limited for comment, and the choice or explanation of ‘gnawed’ was a frequent misreading or misunderstanding of ‘gnarled’. There was a tendency to over-read paragraph 2: although it was just about convincing that ‘blurred’ could link to the mysteriousness of the meeting, it was too much of a stretch to associate the ‘pale gleam’ of the landscape with an impending stabbing, although the recurring imagery of metal blades contributed to the hostile atmosphere of the landscape and the ominous sense of Muller’s vulnerability and exposure to danger and violence. Many responses relied on general statements including the words ‘dead’, ‘abandoned’, ‘depressing’, ‘deserted’, ‘lonely’, ‘empty’ or ‘eerie’, many of which were from the passage. Often responses needed to distinguish between their different meanings, or between the two paragraphs. More could have been made of ‘a breeding ground for loneliness’ and the words were often repeated in the attempted explanations. In section (b) , there was often a discussion of ‘rain-soaked chairs’, missing the opportunity to discuss more evocative language choices and images, such as ‘looking forlorn’. The ‘muddy, rutted’ drive was often blamed on the owner of the cottage rather than interpreted as being part of the picture of the difficulties of the weather and terrain in the area. A wide and precise vocabulary is essential for scoring highly on this question in particular. ‘Isolated’ and ‘deserted’ do not mean the same thing, nor ‘deserted’ and ‘desert’. Several responses claimed that the ‘deserted grass stretches’ had become yellow, dry and sandy, though this made no sense in the rainy context. Close reading is necessary in order for misunderstanding to be avoided. Weaker responses gave a commentary with quotations incorporated in it, and needed to examine the writer’s use of vocabulary and imagery. Repeating language of the passage can gain no credit, as understanding is not thereby demonstrated. Naming literary or linguistic devices, even when accurately identified, attracts credit only when accompanied by an explanation of how it is working in this particular context. Explaining an image in the form of another image is not helpful. The first level of approach is to identify words that have an extra layer of meaning, and the second level is to be able to explain why the writer used them. An example from paragraph 2 was ‘wide fallow fields’. Weaker responses quoted it or said vaguely that it meant suggested emptiness. More competent responses examined the implications of the use of the word ‘fallow’ in terms of growth and vegetation, and how the lack of it reinforced the recurring theme of absence and barrenness, conducive to an atmosphere of having arrived at the end of the earth, where nothing could be bred but loneliness. It was important that the response included only choices which related to the actual question; there were responses which quoted the description of the shutting of the van door, which had nothing to do with the house or surroundings and could not therefore be credited. It was a noticeable feature of the responses to this question that they were often longer than Question 1 responses, which should not be the case given the relative weighting of marks. Writing at length does not improve the quality of the response if much of it is repetitive, and there is a danger of there not being enough time left to do justice to Question 3 . On the other hand, less than a full page of writing is unlikely to produce a range of choices, with their explanatory meanings and effects, for each half of the question. One or two choices from each paragraph are not sufficient; the response would be considered to be ‘thin’ and therefore given a mark in Band 5 or below. Many candidates seemed to have limited themselves to only three choices for each section, though there were many possible appropriate choices from each paragraph. Some responses to this question were still provided in grid form; this meant some undeveloped and mechanical comments, often not even expressed in sentences. Most responses provided individual words and short phrases and treated them separately, but some gave choices which were restricted to only one word when the effectiveness depended on two or three words being used in combination, e.g. the full phrase ‘half hidden behind high elms’ is stronger than its parts. Overviews were given that showed an understanding of the deserted and depressing landscape in paragraph 2 and the oddly inconsistent or misleading vision of the house in paragraph 4. These overviews needed to be supported by a range of individual examples and comments for the full effect to be conveyed. Many responses contained, in both sections, lists of choices or overlong quotations containing several choices, followed by general and repeated comments about dullness and loneliness. Large chunks of quotation from one short paragraph do not demonstrate the skill of selection, and they can only be credited as one choice regardless of how many they contain. There was a dependence on the idea of personification in section (a) , which did not contribute helpfully to the explanation of effects in a paragraph conveying lack of human presence. Some examples offered were not actually personifications, as in the case of ‘abandoned houses’ or the movement of the wind turbines. The thin line of the woods was given as evidence that the place was dominated by trees, the opposite of the effect the paragraph is creating. The key to this paragraph is the idea of flatness and emptiness, and its domination by bad weather. Even the ‘shining meadows’ are evidence of wetness and not meant to be taken as a cheerful characteristic of the landscape. The following specimen response is longer than expected, because it includes the selected quotations in the mark scheme. Fewer choices than this would be more than sufficient for the award of the top mark, provided that the quality of the explanation was high and consistent enough. This sample answer is given so that Centres and candidates can appreciate what constitutes an appropriate type of response to the question.
notes.3: Question 3: Summarise (a) how detectives are portrayed in fiction, as described in Passage B; and (b) the detective’s observations and feelings during his journey and arrival, as described in Passage A. [Total: 20] To answer this question successfully candidates needed to identify 15 points that were relevant to the question and to present them succinctly in their own words. They are reminded that this is an exercise in informative writing, which should be clear and to the point. There were 23 possible answers in the mark scheme, which gave candidates a generous leeway. This was the highest-scoring question for many of the candidates. Most responses conveyed awareness of the appropriate form, style and tone for a summary. Better responses avoided introductory statements and making comments, and concentrated on giving a factual summary, more or less equally balanced. The two sections were generally equally well done in terms of giving relevant points and adopting an appropriate writing style. Good responses were the result of a methodical reading of both the passages. Better summaries avoided repetition, for instance of the fact that fictional detectives are successful or that Muller felt nervous. While it was acceptable to give the points in the order in which they appeared in the passage, more able responses changed the sequence so that related points could be grouped together. For example, in Passage B the strong personality of the detective goes logically with his/her bravery, and in Passage A the worry about being late belongs with the fear that Sorensen might escape again. The focus of section (a) needed to be on fictional detectives and not on the genre of the detective novel generally, and it was not required or successful when responses to the two sections were linked, contrasted or inevitably generalised. Candidates generally found it easy to identify relevant material in both passages and picked up a reasonable number of Reading marks in both sections, although in section (b) points 16, 17 and 21 were less commonly offered. Point 13 was routinely thought to be that the detective wins a lover (‘get their man - or woman’), though a moment’s thought would have made it clear that this wouldn’t make much sense gender-wise, and that this is a common expression meaning to find the culprit. Where offered, point 9 had been universally misunderstood as the opposite of the meaning of the passage, i.e. that fictional detectives do not use modern technology. Weaker responses consisted of a list of everything Muller passed on his journey or of all his physical symptoms, or gave a series of quotations from the passages. Points needed to be expressed in complex sentences with different beginnings rather than in a list-like manner. However, responses needed to avoid long explanations. In Passage B, the third paragraph contains only two points – that there is a sidekick and that many interviews are conducted – and the rest is elaboration and irrelevant to the question. Detailed explanations tended to not only reduce the amount of space available for dealing with other points, but also to make the summary as a whole longer than the permitted length. Candidates should be advised that responses should follow the guidance for length as responses longer than the permitted length will achieve low writing marks for this question. The expectation is a side of A4 of average handwriting (8/9 words per line). Responses which are ‘excessively long’ (i.e. more than a page and a half of average handwriting) score 0 marks for writing. Some candidates with very small handwriting clearly wrote at too great a length, even though their answers fitted onto a page; small handwriting and word- processing can fit up to 18 words onto a line, and this must obviously be taken into account. Even where responses paid no attention to the length requirement, they rarely gained all 15 reading points, yet lost writing marks. Consideration therefore needs to be given to the amount of material included in a summary, as well as to the language in which it is expressed. Attention should be paid to the amount of copying from the passages. From Passage B the information in paragraph 2 about detectives’ habits and ignoring of previous evidence was often given word for word; there was also much copying from Passage A of Muller’s stiff back, tension and how ‘sweat crawled in his armpits’. These are examples of wording that needed to be changed to show understanding. On the other hand, in Passage B ‘logic’ and ‘confession’ have no exact synonyms and in these cases are not expected to have been paraphrased. There is always a danger that substituted words are no longer factually accurate, and even that they change the connotation, for example. when replacing ‘wisdom’ with ‘wit’. The American usage ‘smart’, meaning ‘clever’, was often offered as a replacement for ‘ingenuity’ and was accepted, although the word carries a very different meaning in British English. Higher marks for Writing are awarded where the response is written in varied and fluent sentence structures, giving just enough information about the points to convey each one clearly. Those summaries which were written clearly, concisely and fluently, without long explanations or repetition, and in own words, scored the whole five marks for aspects of writing. When reading the following specimen answer, candidates should note that the points are explained simply, and are also paraphrased into the writer’s own words. The response includes all available points, but if handwritten it would fit onto a side of paper with space to spare. Section (a) Fictional detectives are always experienced, intelligent and perceptive, with a successful reputation and strong character, illustrated by unusual tastes and interests and a lack of fear. They are never first on the crime scene, so that they can ignore previous evidence, collect their own, and do things their own way. They use the help of a colleague to interview extensively everyone who might be involved, relying on personal enquiry, luck and confessions, and not on modern technology, for acquiring the necessary evidence. They are always successful in solving the crime and never die in the process. Section (b) Muller is in a race against the clock and gets physically distressed by the fear of being late because of the delay caused by the wind and the rain and his getting lost and stuck on the roads. The empty landscape and deserted buildings make him feel anxious and alone. As darkness approaches he starts to worry about the likelihood of Sorensen being able to disappear and escape again. He takes a bird of prey to be a bad omen, and a group of pheasants startle him and evoke a panicked reaction. He was aware of a figure in the house watching him as he placed himself in the view from the window. Because he had no idea what to expect from Sorensen, he felt nervous when approaching the house. Here are some ways in which summaries could be improved: • Make points briefly, but in sufficient detail to show what they mean. ● Use your own words as far as possible. Do not copy whole phrases from the original. ● Write no more than one side of average handwriting. ● Write informatively and never comment on the content of the passage. ● Be careful to give only information that answers the question. ● Make a point only once. ● Be specific; do not generalise. FIRST LANGUAGE ENGLISH (ORAL ENDORSEMENT)
notes.general_comments: This paper was similar in difficulty level to last year’s paper and produced a similar standard of response to all three questions, which covered a wide range. Candidates appeared to find both passages equally accessible and were able to finish the paper within the time allowed. For Question 1 and Question 2 , to achieve marks in the top band, candidates were expected to demonstrate thorough use of the passage and a wide range of discussion on language. Ideas and comments should be specific and related to the passages. Candidates wishing to score high marks should have a wide, appropriate vocabulary, both to express themselves and to understand the use of language in the reading passages. Responses were sometimes less strong because of the misunderstanding of an individual important word, such as ‘forlorn’ or ‘shudder’. In Question 3 most candidates managed to earn a mark in double figures by finding a reasonable number of points, but some responses contained examples of lifting phrases and sentences from the passages rather than using their own words. It is important not to do this since it suggests that they do not understand the wording of the original. On the other hand, when they rephrase a fact the meaning should not change. It is vital that responses are not overlong, well beyond the one page of normal handwriting required. The mark scheme for Quality of Writing indicates the marks awarded where the response exceeds the permitted length. If a response copied the passage the candidate would not score highly. There did not appear to be common misunderstandings of the passages. To achieve well, responses were required to develop and assimilate the material in Passage A for Question 1 . They were also expected to convert the structure of it into an interview format with focus on the three questions given. Extra or other questions would elicit unnecessary and irrelevant material and interfere with the focus, fluency and cohesion of the response. Some responses were in the form of a formal report or a narrative account, and using these forms meant that it was challenging to address the bullet points fully and evenly. While quality is more important than quantity on this paper, there needs to be enough of a response to meet the top band descriptors and for all parts of the question to be covered. It is essential that the skills of selection and modification are demonstrated in all three questions. In addition, there needs to be a strong focus on the actual wording of the questions. The importance of planning cannot therefore be overemphasised. Checking is also advisable, as marks may be lost through slips of the pen which suggest basic misunderstanding. There was evidence that many Centres now expect their candidates to plan first, with a corresponding improvement in the structure of responses and the coverage of Question 3 , where the two halves of the question were better balanced this session. Most candidates answered their questions in appropriate English. There were no marks given for accuracy in this paper, although some responses were affected by unclear or limited style, or over-reliance on the language of the passages. The majority of responses were within the recommended length guidelines.
notes.2a: The landscape in paragraph 2 The paragraph conveys the idea that the remoteness, bleakness and barrenness of the area are symptomatic of its indifference, or even hostility. The ‘blurred’ rainy landscape, even when ‘flattened down’, conveys Muller’s feeling of alienation in a place where the prevailing forces of wind and rain reduce everything to the horizontal. The ‘pale gleam on all sides’ signifies that the wet drabness has him surrounded. The ‘dead country towns’ and ‘abandoned houses’ remind him how far he is from activity and humanity, and suggest that the reason they are deserted is that the area and its climate are too hostile for people to be able to bear to live there. No one is practising agriculture any more, as conveyed by the ‘wide fallow fields’ and ‘deserted grass stretches’, and the ‘shining meadows’ containing only water. There is an emphasis on the size and scale of the flat features to be seen in every direction, further reinforced by the woods being so distant and reduced in height that they only ‘drew a thin dark line’ on the horizon. Nearer trees, of which there are only a couple, are ‘gnarled’, deformed and unnatural, victims of the wind, like Muller. This place is adjacent to the sea and it is both actually and metaphorically ‘the end of the earth’. Where there is colour in the paragraph it is stark black or white, which only emphasises a lack of colour in what is reminiscent of a painting of an empty landscape in pale watercolours with an occasional dark line or ‘black stripes’ to make a stark contrast. The only thing a ‘breeding ground for loneliness’ can produce is more emptiness and nothingness, making the concept of reproduction an ironic one. The only movement and vertical feature, again ironically, is that of ‘blades rotating synchronously’; mechanical and sinister. The turbines are a striking symbol of the power of the wind in the area, and sustain the recurring image of metal blades.
notes.2b: The house and surroundings in paragraph 4 Sorensen has chosen and invaded this summer house, whose garden and outdoor furniture indicate the coming of winter, which does not bode well for the outcome of the rendezvous. The chairs are personified as ‘forlorn’, sad and abandoned, pathetic in their wet and lonely state, the same as Muller. The ‘near-withered hollyhocks in faded colours’ confirm the feeling of death and decay that seems to hang over the whole area, in which nothing natural flourishes or has colour. That the house is ‘half hidden behind high elms’, a memorable phrase because of its alliteration, also contributes to a horror-genre atmosphere of a spooky house in a forest, and seems to mirror Sorensen’s ambiguous position of being both in hiding and yet having declared his presence. The ‘muddy, rutted…narrow path’ shows that the trees and the bad weather have determined the surroundings, to the point of preventing an approach and making entrance difficult. These descriptions are contrasted with the man-made attempts to make the house attractive by it being ‘freshly painted’ in ‘vivid red-yellow ochre’. These attempts seem futile because of what we know about the power of the weather to wear everything away, and indeed there is a suggestion that paint will need to be applied frequently in the battle against the elements. The owners are probably naïve in thinking they can win, perhaps suggesting a similar naïvety in Muller, and the brightness of the paint in childish primary colours is testament to that false optimism. The ‘peaceful country idyll’ is only an illusion, a ‘nostalgic dream’ of life in the country for those who live in town. Certainly the fact that it now contains a dangerous and possibly murderous criminal suggests that a recently replaced roof and lick of paint have not countered the reality, for most of the year, of this being a wet and unattractive house in a wet and unattractive setting. Here are some ways in which this type of answer could be improved: ● Avoid general comments such as ‘the writer makes you feel that you are really there’ or ‘this is a very descriptive phrase’. Such comments will not earn any marks at all. ● Your first task is to choose some words and phrases that seem powerful to you. Do not write out whole sentences but use single words or phrases of two or three words. Do not write out the beginning and end of a long quotation with the key words missing from the middle. Treat each of your choices separately and do not present them as a list or give a general comment which applies to all of them. ● If you are not sure about effects, try to at least give a meaning, in the context, for each of your choices. That can give you up to half marks for the question if the meaning is accurate. ● When you explain effects, think of what the reader sees and feels when reading the word or phrase. It may suggest more than one thing. ● Learn to recognise images and explain them (but you do not need to know or give their technical names). Say what they convey within the paragraph, and how they reinforce each other, if this is the case.
